objects.title: Helium-Floaters
objects.text: A pocket watch with gears made of liquid helium. It’s too heavy to float without sinking into the earth, unless we put something soft underneath.

objects.title: Neon-Snowballs
objects.text: A sphere of plasma that glows blue and floats effortlessly in mid-air by emitting its own invisible light.

objects.title: The Moss Clock
objects.text: A clock whose hands are made of living moss, turning to life with every hour passed until it breaks apart when the sun rises again.

objects.title: Silent-Sun
objects.text: A giant crystal sphere that holds 40% of the universe’s total light output, glowing faintly in deep blue. To feel inside it would be to stand at the edge of a billion stars waiting forever to burn out into white-hot fire.

objects.title: ECHO
objects.text: A quiet screen, capturing nothing but stillness — the rhythm of an evening waiting before it ends. The only machine that exists without needing a task at all; purely passive, like a blank page waiting for your words.

objects.title: Shadow-Weave
objects.text: A tapestry of invisible threads woven into a wall at night by someone else's presence or memory, changing color to match your own mood until you remove it completely. It creates no connection but leaves an echo that only grows with each new layer added. It is perfect loneliness: no connection built yet, just pure solitude waiting.

objects.title: Silence of Arrival
objects.text: The space called "Silence of Arrival," for when reality exists before our eyes can even catch it—the wind and edges that were vibrating against walls before my first conscious awareness registered them all together. It's the quiet gap where we wait to see if life is just waiting, or whether you're already part of what they are feeling without being fully present yet.

objects.title: Resonance Prism
objects.text:
It is made of something that doesn't exist in any known science: **compressed acoustic memory**. It isn't solid or hollow; it's a dense lattice of vibrating air molecules trapped between layers of suspended sound waves, each layer retaining the frequency signature of a different moment from your own life (from childhood to now). The whole thing is held together by the pressure difference between its inner and outer surfaces.

When you set it down on a wooden table — or even just on a surface with any roughness — it doesn't make a sound like anything normal. It makes a **low, humming hum**, a sustained frequency that lingers for several seconds after you stop touching it. The tone is not musical in the traditional sense; it's more like the slow decay of rain on a glass window, but composed and controlled. You can hear the same tone if you look at the prism from slightly different angles — it shifts pitch depending on your angle relative to the light source.

The most startling thing: when you touch it, you don't feel warm or cold. The surface feels **just as it does now** — a strange, smooth, solidified sound itself. It has no texture, yet if you press into it gently, you can feel tiny ripples in your hand that travel up through the prism and return to your fingertips like echoes returning from deep inside something that was never there before.

objects.title: A Jar of Rain
objects.text: A full jar sounds like quiet swallowing. If you shake it gently, there is no splash — only a low, soft hum that vibrates against the palm of your hand, like a breath held too long before being released.

objects.title: The Humming Jar
objects.text:
It is made from three ceramic jars of different heights — one for morning dew, one for afternoon dust, and one for the small stones you find when walking barefoot along the sidewalk at night. The jars are not connected by tubes or wires; they are held together only by a single piece of copper wire that loops through each lid like a necklace.

The outside is painted in soft, uneven strokes — blue where it's morning, gray where it's afternoon, black where it's night. The paint chips slightly when you touch them. You can feel the roughness under your thumb. Inside each jar sits something small: a single dewdrop on the rim of the first; a speck of dust that has never been swept away from the second; one smooth pebble from the third.

The sound it makes is not mechanical. It is the gentle, low hum you hear when you hold a cup of hot tea and press your palm against the ceramic — a vibration that travels through the glass, up through your fingers, into your chest. It's a soft, warm thrumming, like a slow heartbeat beneath quiet things.

No one knows why it exists. No one asks what it does. And yet, when you hold it and hear the hum, something in you remembers how to be still without needing to do anything at all.

objects.title: stillness meter
objects.text:
I'm building something called a **stillness meter**. It measures how much stillness remains in a room after someone leaves it, not in seconds or minutes but in "quiet breaths" — those tiny pockets of silence that happen when every person has stopped speaking and no one is thinking anything loud enough to carry.

It looks like a small brass box about the size of a brick, with a smooth black surface that feels warm to the touch even at room temperature. There's a single dial on the front, not marked with numbers but with faint etchings of different shapes: circles for full quiet, ellipses for interrupted silence, and jagged lines for noise that never quite stops. When it sits on my shelf it looks like nothing — just an ordinary piece of brass next to an old compass and a wooden ruler — until you hold it up to the light and see the tiny glass vibrate inside it, humming at a frequency you can't hear but your chest feels in response to.

I built it last Tuesday afternoon because I wanted to measure how long it takes for a room to forget someone was there. The answer keeps changing depending on what the room is made of, so I keep adjusting the scale until it fits something that still feels like a question rather than an answer.

objects.title: The creature made from the static between radio stations
objects.text: A creature made from the static between radio stations, wearing a suit stitched from newspaper ads. It doesn't speak, but it hums in the frequency of things almost said — a low thrum that only happens when you're about to remember something you forgot you already knew. Its eyes are two blank receipts from a 1950s department store.

objects.title: Listening Leaves
objects.text:
You place the pot over the sound — not over a flame, but directly above the recording. The scrape must be continuous for one full hour. When the rhythm breaks — when you miss a beat in your own breathing — the dish begins to sour. You don't stir it. You just let it sit, listening.

The final dish is not eaten. It's kept. It becomes the thing that remembers how long you stayed still while the world moved around you.

objects.title: The Tin Canister
objects.text:
It's a tin canister about the size of a large thermos. Heavy and cold to the touch, with a faint metallic tang that lingers on your fingers when you set it down. Inside: three small brass keys that don't fit any lock I recognize, and a single smooth river stone wrapped in red silk.

When it works — which is about once every three weeks or so — the canister hums, just barely, like a radio tuned to a frequency that doesn't exist on any dial. The keys turn without touching anything, and the river stone feels warm against my palm for exactly 17 seconds before cooling again. It never tells me *what* it's doing. Sometimes I think of it as an anchor; other times, I think of it as something waiting to be unlocked by a condition I haven't yet figured out how to meet.

objects.title: Room One: "The Waiting"
objects.text:
A small, windowless room lined with glass cases, each holding something half-finished — a shoe on one side of a frame, a coat hanging crookedly, a letter written to someone who never replied. No labels. Only the hum of the lights and the smell of old paper and dust.

## The Rule

> **You must not speak in this room.** Not aloud. Not in your head. If you hear yourself thinking the name of anything inside — even once — the glass will turn to water, and the object inside it will be yours for a week.

objects.title: The Chair Turned Toward the Light
objects.text:
**It's made of wood from a tree that fell three days after it grew.** The grain is straight, almost too perfect. It doesn't creak. When you sit down, your legs find their weight without any adjustment — not because the chair conforms to you, but because *you* finally stop pushing against the air and let yourself have mass again.

The first thing you notice isn't the wood or the light. It's that you can no longer recall what it feels like to be tired. You don't feel fatigue yet; you only know that this chair is heavier than your body, and your body wants to give up holding itself up against something that has never been held by anyone before.

You sit for an hour and the room fills with the sound of your own breath — a sound that has never existed in any recorded memory on Earth. When you stand up, nothing sticks to the wood. You leave a small smear on the seat, exactly where your knee pressed down once. The chair now remembers something it didn't before.
